To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the variance risk premium is positively related to the size of the impact of return shocks on conditional volatility, (2) the variance risk premia is positively related to how the impact of return shock on conditional volatility differs for negative and positive shocks, (3) the implied volatility smile is negatively related to the impact of negative (positive) shocks on future volatility, and (4) differences in the impact of return on future volatility explain much, but again not all, of variations in excess

the size of the implied volatility slope and the variance risk premium are related to how volatility responds to shocks in the past and that the size of excess kurtosis is related to how volatility changes when the return shock is negative.

(i) the variance risk premium is larger in markets in which return shocks have large impacts on future conditional volatility and in which negative shocks have a larger impact than positive shocks, (ii) the implied volatility smile is more downward sloping in markets in which negative return shocks have a larger than average impact on future volatility and in which the impact of negative shocks on future volatility is larger than the impact of positive shocks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cross-sectional relation between the shape of the option implied volatility smile, the variance risk premium, and parameters of GARCH type models.
how the shape of an option's implied volatility smile relates to the time-series dynamics of conditional volatility.
how conditional volatility and the implied volatility smile are related, and we find that they are indeed related in a systematic manner.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
markets in which volatility increases more in response to negative return shocks than to positive return shocks tend to be characterized by downward sloping implied volatility curves.

the shape of the volatility smile is related to the shape of the response function of volatility to shocks and the magnitude of the variance risk premia is related to the magnitude of the response function.
the cross-sectional patterns in volatility and the implied volatility smile can be explained by the cross-sectional patterns of the GARCH-type time series models.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we find a cross-sectional relationship between the shape of the volatility smile and the time-series behavior of conditional volatility.
the shape of the volatility smile and the magnitude of the variance risk premia reflect how the market prices the future response of volatility to return shocks.

markets in which return shocks have large impacts on future conditional volatility tend to exhibit large variance risk premia, large kurtosis, and upward sloping (downward sloping) smiles when the return shocks are positive (negative).
The main takeaway from our work is that

the cross-sectional variation in the implied volatility smile, the variance risk premium, and the shape of the return distribution is related to how conditional volatility responds in time-series models.
the shape of the smile and the magnitude of the variance risk premia are related to the same factors that determine the time-series behavior of conditional volatility.
GARCH-type models can be used to explain a large part of the variations in both the implied volatility smile shape and the variance risk premium across different markets.
